books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text:
President James Monroe spoke to Congress on December 2, 1823:

“. . . the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers. . . . We owe it, therefore, to candor and to the amicable relations existing between the United States and those powers to declare that we should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety. With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.”
stimulus.source_note: James Monroe, seventh annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823; wording verified against the Avalon Project, Yale Law School. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The Monroe Doctrine is best described as a policy of

options.text: American intervention in every war in Europe
options.misconception: Monroe says the United States will stay out of Europe's quarrels.

options.text: mutual noninterference between the United States and Europe
a military alliance with the new Latin American republics
options.misconception: No alliance was signed with any Latin American republic.

options.text: annexation of the remaining Spanish colonies
options.misconception: The United States annexed nothing in 1823.

rationales.A: The Doctrine's other half is that the United States will not meddle in Europe. Intervention in European wars is the opposite of its bargain.
rationales.B: Monroe's deal runs both ways: Europe stays out of the Americas, and the United States stays out of Europe's affairs and leaves existing colonies alone.
rationales.C: No treaty of alliance was signed. The Doctrine was a unilateral American statement, not a military pact.
rationales.D: Monroe warned Europe against new colonies; he did not claim Spanish colonies for the United States.
rationales.general:
1. Read the American side. Europe must not colonize or extend its system in the Americas.
2. Read the European side. The United States will not interfere with existing colonies, and it stays out of Europe's affairs.
3. Put it together. Each side stays out of the other's sphere: mutual noninterference.
Background: The Doctrine became a cornerstone of American foreign policy alongside Washington's Farewell Address.
Remember: when a policy tells both sides to stay out, it is a bargain of noninterference, not a conquest.
